Baby & Child

Hydranencephaly: signs, diagnosis and supportive care

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hydranencephaly is a rare, severe condition present from birth in which almost all of the two cerebral hemispheres are absent and replaced by fluid. A specialist team can explain the diagnosis, plan care around the child’s needs and support the family through uncertain decisions.

What the diagnosis means

The cerebral hemispheres support thinking, voluntary movement and many sensory functions. In hydranencephaly, much of this tissue has been destroyed or disrupted during development. The skull and some deeper structures, often including the brainstem and cerebellum, remain; it does not mean every part of the forebrain or the entire brain is absent.

Cerebrospinal fluid normally cushions the brain and spinal cord. Here it occupies the space left by missing tissue; it is not, by definition, a substance that blocks the brain. Hydranencephaly differs from severe hydrocephalus, where enlarged fluid spaces still surround a remaining layer of cerebral tissue, and from anencephaly.

Signs may appear at birth or later

Some babies initially have apparently normal reflexes or head size because lower brain structures still function. Others are affected from birth, or develop clearer difficulties over weeks or months. Head size can become unusually large when fluid accumulates, but a large head is not present in every case and cannot establish this diagnosis.

Possible problems include seizures or involuntary movements, stiffness or altered muscle tone with limited movement, severe developmental impairment, vision or hearing difficulties, poor feeding and growth, breathing or digestive problems, and difficulty regulating temperature. New symptoms deserve assessment rather than being attributed automatically to the existing condition.

Causes and questions about inheritance

The exact cause is often uncertain. A leading explanation is interruption of blood flow to the developing cerebral hemispheres, including the internal carotid circulation. Prenatal infections and other vascular events have also been associated with some cases. A suggested exposure or association does not prove what caused an individual child’s condition or establish parental fault.

Most cases are sporadic. Rare genetic disorders, including Fowler syndrome, can involve hydranencephaly, so inheritance and recurrence require individual specialist and genetic counseling. A team may consider targeted infection or genetic investigations and imaging in a future pregnancy. There is no proven general measure that guarantees prevention.

How specialists confirm it

Prenatal ultrasound, sometimes with detailed fetal brain assessment and fetal MRI, may identify the problem. After birth, cranial ultrasound and particularly MRI help show which structures remain. Specialist interpretation distinguishes hydranencephaly from extreme hydrocephalus, holoprosencephaly and other conditions with different anatomy and implications.

Passing light through an infant’s skull, called transillumination, is a historical or supplementary observation, not a home test or a substitute for imaging. CT or blood-vessel imaging may be used for selected questions; contrast angiography and radiation-based scans are not automatic tests for every baby.

Breathing, movement and everyday comfort

Breathing problems need their own assessment, including possible swallowing-related aspiration, infection or impaired neurological control. “Reactive airway disease” is a nonspecific label for asthma-like symptoms before a clear diagnosis; it is neither a synonym for COPD nor an inevitable complication of hydranencephaly. Treatment depends on the actual problem.

Severe movement and muscle-tone difficulties may overlap with cerebral palsy patterns. Physiotherapy, positioning, sensory assessment and comfort care should match the child’s needs. Constipation may be worsened by limited mobility, feeding difficulties or medicines; a pediatric bowel plan may include prescribed laxatives. Irritability may signal pain, muscle spasms, digestive discomfort, infection or raised pressure and should not simply be dismissed.

Feeding, growth and water-balance problems

Feeding can be difficult because of impaired coordination or swallowing. Nutrition and swallowing specialists can assess growth, aspiration risk, suitable feeding methods and whether tube feeding would help. These decisions should reflect safety, comfort and family goals; forcing feeds or changing the diet without advice can create risks.

Central diabetes insipidus, also called arginine vasopressin deficiency, has been reported in some affected children. The brain’s hormone signal to conserve water is insufficient; this differs from a primary kidney response problem and from diabetes mellitus. Unusually large amounts of dilute urine, very wet nappies, thirst or dehydration need prompt assessment of fluid balance and sodium. Do not restrict fluids or start hormone treatment yourself; pediatric endocrine care individualizes treatment.

Treatment supports needs; a shunt has limits

There is no treatment that restores the missing cerebral hemispheres. Care may involve pediatrics, neurology, neurosurgery, rehabilitation, respiratory, nutrition and palliative-care teams. Palliative care can provide symptom relief and family support alongside other treatment, with decisions guided by comfort, expected benefit and the family’s values.

If fluid pressure or progressive head enlargement causes problems, selected children may benefit from a shunt that drains fluid, often to the abdomen. This can relieve pressure but does not rebuild brain tissue or guarantee longer life or improved development. Blockage, infection and repeat operations are possible. Other fluid-control procedures are specialist options for selected situations, not universal alternatives or cures.

Seizures and medication planning

A neurologist can prescribe antiseizure treatment and an individualized emergency plan, including rescue medicine when appropriate and caregiver training. Calming routines may improve comfort but are not seizure treatment. A ketogenic diet is a specialist treatment for selected epilepsies, never a diet to start independently in a child with feeding or fluid-balance problems.

Keep a coordinated medicine list and discuss benefits, adverse effects, constipation and interactions with the child’s team. Do not stop antiseizure medicines or add laxatives, sedatives or supplements without advice. Record episodes and their duration when it is safe; during a seizure protect the child from injury, put nothing in the mouth and do not offer food or drink before full recovery.

When to get urgent help

Seek emergency help immediately for a first seizure, a seizure reaching five minutes or lasting longer than the child’s usual pattern or emergency-plan threshold, repeated seizures without recovery, serious injury, blue or grey coloring, severe breathing difficulty or unresponsiveness. Follow the rescue plan while help is arranged; a first seizure or breathing problem is not a reason to wait five minutes.

Contact the child’s team immediately for possible shunt trouble, including new vomiting, marked sleepiness or irritability, fever, redness or tenderness along the shunt, or rapid head change. New poor feeding, a tense or bulging soft spot, unusual temperature or possible dehydration also needs urgent assessment. If the child is very ill, difficult to wake or struggling to breathe, use emergency care. Follow any more specific team instructions promptly.

Outlook and support for the family

Hydranencephaly is life-limiting and usually causes profound neurological impairment. Death can occur before birth or in infancy, while some children live for years and occasional much longer survival is reported. Limited case reports and selected retrospective cohorts cannot provide a reliable personal deadline or prove that one procedure causes longer survival. Ask the team what is known and uncertain for this child.

Families deserve clear conversations about pregnancy or birth planning, ongoing treatment goals, comfort, practical care, respite, psychological support and bereavement support when relevant. Qualified rare-disease organizations may help find peer support and research information, but a listing does not mean a suitable trial is available or a cure is imminent. The child’s comfort, interactions and the family’s priorities remain central.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

AAP’s June 2025 educational review and ISUOG’s written specialist resource support imaging-based diagnosis, usually sporadic causation with rare genetic forms, and individualized supportive and palliative care.

Reports of central diabetes insipidus and longer survival are limited; case series cannot establish universal complication rates, personal survival deadlines or a causal survival benefit from shunting.

Current NHS emergency instructions support prompt action for first or prolonged seizures and possible shunt infection or blockage; the child’s own rescue and care plans remain essential.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize questions and records of feeding, wet nappies, medicines and episodes for appointments. It cannot interpret brain scans, assess pressure or dehydration, or replace the child’s emergency plan. Urgent symptoms take priority over tracking.

When to seek help

Emergency help is needed for a first or prolonged seizure, repeated seizures without recovery, severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey coloring or unresponsiveness. Possible shunt problems require immediate contact with the team; use emergency care if the child is very ill. Do not change medicines, feeds or fluids without clinical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Specialist brain imaging confirms the anatomy; head size or a light test alone cannot diagnose hydranencephaly.
  • Care includes breathing, movement, feeding, bowel, seizure and sometimes hormone needs, individualized for the child.
  • A shunt can relieve selected pressure problems but cannot restore missing brain tissue or promise survival.
  • Use the child’s emergency plan and seek immediate help for seizures, breathing difficulty, unresponsiveness or suspected serious shunt problems.

Frequently asked questions

What signs can hydranencephaly cause?

Signs include seizures, altered muscle tone and movement, severe developmental difficulties, sensory problems, poor feeding or growth, and breathing, digestion or temperature-control problems. Some emerge later; head size alone does not establish the diagnosis.

Is hydranencephaly always inherited?

No. Most cases are sporadic and the cause may remain uncertain. Vascular injury is a leading explanation; rare genetic forms exist. Genetic counseling can discuss appropriate investigations and recurrence for the individual family.

How is it diagnosed?

Specialists use prenatal ultrasound and sometimes fetal MRI, or cranial ultrasound and MRI after birth. They distinguish other severe brain conditions. A flashlight test is not enough, and CT or angiography is reserved for selected questions.

Can hydranencephaly be cured?

Missing cerebral tissue cannot currently be restored. Treatment aims to relieve symptoms and support safety and comfort. Seizure medicines, feeding support and selected pressure-relieving procedures may help particular needs; none guarantees a cure or a fixed lifespan.

Does every child need a shunt?

No. Neurosurgeons consider symptoms, pressure, progressive head growth and the goals of care. Shunts can block or become infected, and may need revision. New vomiting, sleepiness, fever or shunt redness needs immediate contact with the care team.

Why might a child pass very large amounts of urine?

Central diabetes insipidus is one possible cause: too little vasopressin signal allows excessive water loss. It is not diabetes mellitus. Very wet nappies or dehydration require prompt assessment; do not restrict fluids or treat this yourself.

When is a seizure an emergency?

Get emergency help for a first seizure, one reaching five minutes or exceeding the usual pattern or care-plan threshold, repeated seizures without recovery, injury or breathing problems. Follow the prescribed rescue plan; do not wait five minutes for a first seizure or breathing difficulty.

Can anyone predict exactly how long a child will live?

No. The condition is severe and life-limiting, but experiences differ and available studies are limited. Some deaths occur before birth or in infancy; longer survival also occurs. The clinical team can discuss individual uncertainties, support and goals.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
